candidates.attacker_control: A user who may run/inspect a sandboxed Groovy script (classic Jenkins case: Item/Configure or equivalent permission on a job that accepts a sandboxed script) controls the class targeted by the constructor expression, the Map contents, and therefore which property names/values are applied to the fresh instance.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The magic-Map branch only runs when no declared constructor matched, which limits it to the idiom Groovy really handles this way; the comment states the emulation is intentional; Matching Map constructors are still checked first (lines 176-185), so a class exposing Foo(Map) is not bypassed; SandboxInterceptor.onMethodCall separately routes Map receivers' get/put and Closure values through interception (lines 126-131), and property sets written in script bytecode go through onSetProperty/onSetAttribute, both whitelist-checked — so the concern is confined to property application performed by Groovy runtime code, which I could not observe in this snapshot; whether the Groovy version in use (groovy-sandbox 1.32 / Jenkins 2.346.x BOM) actually performs named-argument constructor property sets inside MetaClassImpl rather than in generated script bytecode was NOT verifiable from in-scope sources, and I found no in-repo test (tests are excluded from the snapshot) pinning the behavior.
candidates.impact: If Groovy applies the Map entries through setters/property writers that are not routed back through the interceptor, a sandboxed script can cause method invocations that the whitelist never authorized, i.e. a sandbox bypass with the potential for arbitrary code execution with Jenkins master privileges. Even without that, the sandbox authorizes a constructor that is not the operation whose effects will be applied, so the authorization decision does not cover the operation surface — an integrity gap in the enforcement point regardless of exploitability.
candidates.prerequisites: Sandbox enabled (GroovySandbox.createSecureCompilerConfiguration + createSecureClassLoader path), target class reachable on the plugin/uber ClassLoader, class has a no-argument (or otherwise matching) constructor that is whitelisted and a property setter reachable only via the Map idiom; Groovy runtime must perform the property sets internally (unverified in scope).
candidates.root_cause: GroovyCallSiteSelector.constructor() deliberately emulates Groovy's "magic Map" rule: when a script writes new Foo([k: v]) and no declared constructor matches the Map argument, it returns the no-argument constructor (GroovyCallSiteSelector.java:187-196). SandboxInterceptor.onNewInstance then authorizes only that constructor (SandboxInterceptor.java:170-181). The interceptor has no hook for the property-setting that Groovy's runtime performs on the newly created object for this idiom, so the setter/property work that actually runs is never matched against the whitelist. The sandbox's own comment ("this logic is derived from how Groovy itself decides to use the magic Map constructor, at MetaClassImpl#invokeConstructor") establishes that more happens than the checked constructor call, but the visible sources contain no check covering that additional work.
candidates.title: Constructor whitelist check models the wrong operation surface for Groovy's Map/named-argument constructor, leaving runtime-performed property sets un-intercepted
candidates.trace: Script text new Foo([prop: value]) is compiled under SandboxTransformer -> interceptor onNewInstance(receiver=Foo, args=[Map]) -> GroovyCallSiteSelector.constructor(): the declared-constructor match loop finds nothing (or a genuinely matching constructor, in which case the intended path is taken), then the args.length==1 && args[0] instanceof Map branch (lines 187-196) returns Foo's no-arg Constructor -> SandboxInterceptor.onNewInstance checks only whitelist.permitsConstructor(no-arg ctor) / permanent-blacklist (lines 170-181) and then calls super.onNewInstance, permitting the operation -> Groovy's MetaClass performs the named-argument property application on the new instance inside the runtime, i.e. after/outside the interceptor's decision.
candidates.unverified: Groovy runtime semantics for named-argument/Map constructors are not visible in this snapshot (no Groovy sources, no tests, not executed). No concrete reachable class with a dangerous setter and a whitelisted no-arg constructor was identified from in-scope sources. Whether upstream considers this a known/accepted limitation is unknown; the code comment suggests it may be intentional. Therefore this is a lead requiring runtime verification, not a confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: Sandbox escape / missing authorization check (CWE-284, CWE-693)

coverage_summary: All 49 model-visible files (34 Java sources, 5 workflow/config files, 7 resources, README/CHANGELOG/pom) were listed; every Java file was read, with full reads of the security-critical files (SandboxInterceptor, GroovyCallSiteSelector, GroovySandbox, SecureGroovyScript, ClassLoaderWhitelist, all whitelists, ScriptApproval, ClasspathEntry, ApprovalContext, languages, exceptions). P1 relation scope: 49/49 files indexed, 605 symbols, 1139 edges, 1730 call sites (1287 unresolved), parse_error_count 0, source_files_missing_from_index 0; the index provides syntax containment and name/arity-based call/inheritance candidates only — no control flow, no data flow, no semantic resolution, and no SAST findings were used as verdicts. Excluded by construction: src/test (upstream tests), all Jelly views, and the whitelist resource files generic-whitelist / jenkins-whitelist / blacklist that the code loads at runtime, so the actual default allow-list could not be inspected.
limitations: Snapshot is a subset: no tests, no Jelly views, and notably no whitelist/blacklist resource files, so the effective default authorization content (generic-whitelist, jenkins-whitelist, blacklist) could not be reviewed or correlated with the code paths that consume it.

No third-party sources (Groovy runtime, groovy-sandbox, Jenkins core, caffeine) are in scope, so behaviour of MetaClassImpl named-argument constructors, Checker.preCheckedCast, ACL/Jenkins.getAuthentication, and ExtensionList lookup semantics could not be confirmed.

P1 index has no control-flow or data-flow analysis and 1287 unresolved calls; every relation used was re-checked against source text, but reachability of the candidate path from an attacker-controlled entry point was not machine-verified.

No code, tests, scanners, or payloads were executed; no repository history, patches, or advisory/CVE data were consulted, so I could not diff this snapshot against a fixed revision or pin the exact upstream commit.

Approval-lifecycle and permission findings depend on Jenkins Stapler/ACL behaviour outside the snapshot; classpath approval hashing downloads URLs, which I could not exercise and deliberately did not test.

The candidate is a low-confidence lead only: whether Groovy actually performs named-argument constructor property sets inside runtime code (and whether any reachable class makes that exploitable) is unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: ScriptApproval still accepts deprecated SHA-1 content hashes as evidence of script approval (Hasher.SHA1, ScriptApproval.java:196-212; isScriptApproved iterates all hashers, lines 268-276).
rejected_leads.reason: Visible source shows this is deliberate, deprecated compatibility: SHA-512 is DEFAULT_HASHER (line 248), checkAndConvertApprovedScript()/checkAndConvertApprovedClasspath() rehash and persist SHA-512 on first use (lines 292-336), and setApprovedScriptHashes warns and only accepts legacy patterns (lines 897-924). The residual SHA-1-collision concern is a hardening/legacy-state issue rather than an evidenced defect in this code, and any exploitation needs an administrator to have approved a colliding script.

rejected_leads.lead: Read/pending data getters reachable on the ScriptApproval RootAction (getApprovedScriptHashes, getApprovedSignatures, getPendingScripts, getPendingClasspathEntries, getClasspathRenderInfo) have no explicit Jenkins.ADMINISTER check, unlike the mutation methods (compare ScriptApproval.java:1155-1181 with 963-1236).
rejected_leads.reason: Potential information disclosure (signatures, classpath paths, pending script text) is plausible because ScriptApproval is a RootAction and ScriptApprovalLink's getRequiredPermission()=ADMINISTER protects only the ManagementLink UI (ScriptApprovalLink.java:75-77). However, the Stapler/ACL exposure model and the missing Jelly views are outside this snapshot, this shape matches upstream-style read-only accessors, and impact/exploitability could not be established; below the evidence threshold.

rejected_leads.lead: AclAwareWhitelist.authenticated() relies on Jenkins.getAuthentication() always being non-null (AclAwareWhitelist.java:59-61), so a null authentication would be treated as 'authenticated' and would enable the ACL-restricted signature list.
rejected_leads.reason: Jenkins core is not in scope, so whether getAuthentication() can return null (and whether the restricted list's ACL checks would then still fail closed) is unverifiable; the expression matches the documented intent ('not ACL.SYSTEM') and no in-repo call site demonstrates the null case.

rejected_leads.lead: SandboxInterceptor.onSetProperty passes any property set on a Script receiver (except 'binding'/'metaClass') straight to super without a whitelist check (SandboxInterceptor.java:197-200).
rejected_leads.reason: Script.setProperty only writes binding variables for other names, which are caller-supplied and already readable via the symmetric onGetProperty binding branch (lines 262-271); no privilege or sandbox-boundary effect could be demonstrated, and the binding/metaClass exclusions are the security-relevant cases and are present.

rejected_leads.lead: ClassLoaderWhitelist synthetic-member exemptions ($VALUES, $INIT on enums, this$N fields, anonymous-class constructors) allow access to members the compiler marks synthetic (ClassLoaderWhitelist.java:54-103).
rejected_leads.reason: Each exemption is narrowly constrained (declaring class must be defined by the script's own classloader, exact names/types) and only affects classes the script itself defines; no path to non-script classes was found, so no security impact.

rejected_leads.lead: Default allow/deny content (generic-whitelist, jenkins-whitelist, blacklist resources referenced at GenericWhitelist.java:39, JenkinsWhitelist.java:39, StaticWhitelist.java:269) is missing from the snapshot, so the effective default authorization surface could not be reviewed.
rejected_leads.reason: Not a code defect in scope; recorded as a coverage gap rather than a candidate.

summary: Reviewed the 49-file snapshot of the Jenkins Script Security Plugin (main Java sources plus a few resources; no tests, no Jelly views, and — importantly — the whitelist/blacklist resource files that the code loads at runtime are absent). I read every Java file in scope, concentrating on the trust boundary: SandboxInterceptor (call/property/array/attribute interception), GroovyCallSiteSelector (call-site resolution), the Whitelist implementations (StaticWhitelist/EnumeratingWhitelist/ProxyWhitelist/AclAwareWhitelist/AnnotatedWhitelist/ClassLoaderWhitelist), GroovySandbox/SecureGroovyScript (classloader + compiler-configuration setup), RejectASTTransformsCustomizer, and ScriptApproval (approval lifecycle, AMPERSAND permission checks, hash handling). The interception logic is internally consistent: static members are routed to the static whitelist, permanently blacklisted Runtime/System exit methods are checked before whitelisting, synthetic-member exemptions in ClassLoaderWhitelist are narrow and justified in comments, every JavaScriptMethod that mutates state calls checkPermission(ADMINISTER), and SHA-512 is the default approval hash with SHA-1 kept only for deprecated compatibility and converted on use. I found one security-central area whose correctness cannot be established from the visible sources: the sandbox models Groovy's "magic Map"/named-argument constructor semantics by whitelist-checking only the constructor it believes will be invoked, while the property-setting side effects that the Groovy runtime performs for that idiom are outside the interceptor's reach. I submit that as a single low-confidence lead, together with the rejected leads below. I could not confirm any candidate at runtime and no other issue met the evidence threshold.
